prime.problem: Waiting times, time-to-next-request and decay are everywhere, and you need to answer "how long until the first of several finishes?" or "I've already waited 5 minutes, how much longer?" without integrals. Guess with intuition and you'll assume waiting brings the end closer, which for these processes it doesn't.
prime.fits: It follows the Pareto card's ratio S(b)/S(a), now with an exponential tail, and is the continuous twin of cs-8's geometric. The Weibull, order-statistics, deductible and normal-approximation cards all lean on it.
expect: rate λ vs mean 1/λ (and which one a library wants)
memorylessness as a ratio of tails
min of independent exponentials: rates add
prime.goal: Answer tail, conditional and "which finishes first" questions for exponential waits in one line each, prove memorylessness from the tail, and say when an exponential is the wrong model for a duration.

attend: Why does the pharmacy order run past its own mean only 37% of the time, not 50%?
In the memoryless proof, which event sits inside which, and why does s cancel?
Why does the minimum of two counters have mean 5 minutes, not 10, and what assumption makes the tails multiply?
How do the gamma and the Weibull with shape ½ break memorylessness in opposite directions?

must: Events at a constant rate λ, independently → P(no event in [0, x]) = e−λx → the tail is one exponential, so every tail question is one exp call (e−1 = 0.3679 at the pharmacy)

{X > s + t} ⊂ {X > s} → P(X > s + t | X > s) = e<sup>−λ(s+t)</sup>/e<sup>−λs</sup> = e<sup>−λt</sup> → time already waited cancels → memoryless, constant hazard λ; the only continuous law with this property
min > x only if every clock is > x → with independence the tails multiply → e<sup>−(λ₁+…+λₙ)x</sup> → the first finisher is Exp(sum of rates) and clock i wins with probability λ<sub>i</sub>/Σλ
elevated: Rate vs scale parameterisation → random.expovariate takes λ, numpy's exponential takes 1/λ → passing the pharmacy's mean 10 where the rate belongs silently simulates waits of mean 0.1 min, 100× too short
reference: the MGF λ/(λ − t) for t < λ
the log-survival straight-line check on real data

compress.prompt: From memory, write the three one-line results of this card (tail, memoryless, minimum) and draw one arrow chain from "constant rate" to "memoryless". Add one sentence on when the model is wrong.
checklist: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t): the s cancels in the ratio
min of independent exponentials is Exp(Σλ); P(i first) = λ<sub>i</sub>/Σλ
wrong for durations that wear out (gamma, Weibull k > 1) or heavy-tailed jobs (Pareto)

retrieve.q: Explain memorylessness in terms of the survival function, and why the uniform on (0, 20) with the same mean fails it.
answer: conditional survival is a ratio S(s + t)/S(s)
for e<sup>−λx</sup> the ratio is e<sup>−λt</sup>, free of s
for U(0, 20), P(X > 20 | X > 10) = 0: a hard limit means waiting brings the end closer

retrieve.q: Two pharmacy counters, each Exp(mean 10), both busy. Walk through the distribution of the time until the first frees up, and the chance each one is first.
answer: so the first finish is Exp(0.2), mean 5 min, P(min > 10) = e<sup>−2</sup> = 0.1353
each counter is first with probability 0.1/0.2 = 1/2

retrieve.q: You're modelling job durations for a queue. When is an exponential a good choice, and what does it cost you if the jobs actually wear out (rising hazard)?
answer: good: gaps between independent arrivals at a constant rate; it makes "which first" and queueing math easy
if jobs wear out, the exponential overstates the chance of very long jobs and understates how predictable a job that's running long is
the gamma(2, 5) example: P(X > 20 | X > 10) = 0.2256, not 0.3679

compare.q: The geometric and the exponential are both memoryless. What's the continuous/discrete difference in the proof, and when would you use each?
answer: geometric: P(X > s + t | X > s) = (1 − p)<sup>t</sup>, trials counted in whole numbers
exponential: the same ratio with e<sup>−λt</sup>, time measured continuously
use the geometric for counts of trials, the exponential for clock time; the exponential is the limit of many tiny trials

compare.q: Exponential vs Weibull: which parameter turns one into the other, what does it do to the hazard, and how does each fail on a part that wears out?
answer: the Weibull with shape k = 1 is the exponential
k > 1 makes the hazard rise with age, k < 1 makes it fall; the exponential's is flat
the exponential fails on wear-out by being memoryless; the Weibull fails on a bathtub-shaped hazard, since its hazard only moves one way

predict.q: Three counters with rates 0.1, 0.1 and 0.2 per minute are all busy. You've already waited 4 minutes and none has finished. What is the expected extra wait for the first one, and which counter is most likely to finish first?
predict.answer: Memorylessness makes the 4 minutes irrelevant: the minimum is Exp(0.1 + 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.4), so the expected extra wait is 1/0.4 = 2.5 minutes. The rate-0.2 counter finishes first with probability 0.2/0.4 = 1/2; each of the others with 1/4.

apply.task: Two counters with different speeds: rates 0.1 and 0.2 per minute. By hand, find (a) the mean time until the first finishes, (b) the chance the faster one finishes first, (c) P(first finish > 10 min). Then check all three with a 10⁶-pair simulation using random.expovariate (rate, not mean).
apply.done: Hand answers 1/0.3 = 3.33 min, 2/3, and e<sup>−3</sup> = 0.0498, and your simulation lands within a few thousandths of each.
apply.hint: Rates add for the minimum; the winner's chance is its share of the total rate.
